Likewise, the import methods `importData()`, `importObject()`, `importFromJSON()`, `importFromCSV()`, and its helper `processCsvImport()` all overwrite or populate `this.leaves`, `this.stem`, and `this.tags` in memory but contain no call to `saveData()` anywhere in their bodies, so imported data is never written to `dataFile` regardless of `autoSave`. `loadData()` inherits this gap on its normal path since it calls `importData()` when the file exists, though its no-file fallback calls `initializeDefaultData()`, which does save.

Rosemary#connectLeaves checks `this.leaves.has(id)` for each id and throws `Error("Leaf with id <id> not found")` for an unknown or missing/undefined id, but for identical ids it instead just `console.warn`s "Cannot connect a leaf to itself." and returns early with no connection made and no error thrown; relationshipType defaults to `''` and is stored unvalidated. The CLI's `connect <id1> <id2>` declares both ids as required Commander arguments, so a truly missing id is rejected by Commander itself before `connectLeaves` runs, while an unknown id reaches `connectLeaves`, throws, and is caught in the action's try/catch to print the error via `chalk.red`; because the same-id case doesn't throw, the CLI still logs "Connected leaf..." and calls `saveData()` as if it succeeded, and its `-r/--relationship` option defaults to `''` via `options.relationship || ''`. `POST /api/v1/connect` destructures `id1, id2, type` from `req.body` with no presence validation, so a missing id becomes `undefined`, hitting either the same-id no-op (if both ids end up equal/absent) or the "not found" throw; any thrown error (unknown or missing id) is caught and returned as `400 {error: message}`, while duplicate ids get a `200 {message: 'Leaves connected successfully'}` response despite nothing being connected. The API passes `req.body.type` through untouched, relying on `connectLeaves`'s own `''` default when it is absent. In short, only the duplicate-id case is silently swallowed at every layer; unknown/missing ids surface as thrown errors that the CLI prints and the API turns into 400s (except when a missing id collides into the same-id branch), and relationship type is optional and unvalidated throughout.

Only Rosemary#connectLeaves validates anything: an unknown leaf id makes it throw "Leaf with id X not found," the same id given twice makes it log a warning ("Cannot connect a leaf to itself.") and return without connecting, and any relationship-type string is accepted and stored as given, defaulting to an empty string if omitted. The CLI's connect command relies on commander to refuse to run at all if either id argument is missing, but otherwise just surfaces connectLeaves' behavior: an unknown id prints its thrown message in red and exits 0, and the same id twice is reported as success; it never validates the relationship type either. The REST API's POST /api/v1/connect does not validate its request body at all, so a single missing id reaches connectLeaves and is treated like an unknown id (400 "not found"), while two missing ids are indistinguishable from passing the same id twice (200, nothing connected); an unknown id otherwise returns 400 with connectLeaves' message, and the relationship type is passed through unvalidated in all three layers.

Only Rosemary#connectLeaves validates anything: an unknown leaf id makes it throw "Leaf with id X not found", which the CLI prints in red (still exiting 0) while the API turns into a 400 response carrying that message. Passing the same id twice makes connectLeaves log a warning ("Cannot connect a leaf to itself.") and return without creating a connection, yet both the CLI and the API report success in that case. For a missing id, commander itself rejects `rosemary connect` unless both ids are supplied, but the API never validates the request body: two missing ids resolve as "same id" and return 200 with nothing connected, while exactly one missing id produces a 400 "not found" error. The relationship type is never validated anywhere in the chain—any string is accepted and stored as given, defaulting to an empty string when omitted.

`npm run release -- patch` runs the `release` npm script (`package.json`), which invokes `scripts/release.js`: it first aborts if `git status --porcelain` shows uncommitted changes, then aborts if the branch isn't `main` (unless `--force-branch`), then runs the test suite via `npm test --silent`. It then runs `npm version patch` (bumps `package.json` and creates git tag `v<version>` with commit message `chore(release): %s`), followed by `git push --follow-tags` to push the commit and tag to origin. Finally `scripts/release.js` runs `npm publish`, which triggers the `prepublishOnly` npm script in `package.json` (`npm test && node scripts/check-release.js`). `scripts/check-release.js` re-checks: working tree clean, HEAD matches tag `v<version>`, tag exists on origin, version not already on the npm registry, and `CHANGELOG.md` mentions the version — exiting non-zero on any failure. If `check-release.js` passes, `npm publish` proceeds and uploads the package to the npm registry.

Only once check-release.js exits 0 does npm actually publish the package to the registry.

In `scoreContextRelevance`, each related leaf's relevance = min(1, distanceScore + tagScore + relationshipScore + recencyScore + semanticScore) rounded to 3 decimals, where distanceScore = 1/max(distance,1) (weight 1, no cap), tagScore = min(sharedTags * 0.15, 0.3) (0.15 per shared tag, capped 0.3), relationshipScore = 0.2 if a relationship type exists else 0, recencyScore = max(0, 0.1 - ageDays*0.002) (starts at 0.1, decays 0.002/day), and semanticScore = cosineSimilarity(centerEmbedding, leafEmbedding) * 0.2 only if both embeddings exist (else 0). `buildPromptContext` sorts `related` by this relevance (desc, then by distance asc) before calling `pruneToTokenLimit(context, maxTokens)`. `pruneToTokenLimit` first estimates tokens and returns immediately if already within `maxTokens`; otherwise it (1) re-sorts `related` by relevance descending and filters out any leaf with relevance below 0.5, re-estimating and returning if now within budget; (2) if still over, slices `related` down to the top 3 entries, re-estimating and returning if within budget; (3) if still over, deletes `core.tags`; then returns the clone regardless of the final size (no further reduction is attempted).

`scoreContextRelevance` sums five terms then clamps to at most 1 (rounded to 3 decimals): distance score `1/max(distance,1)` (unweighted), `0.15` per shared tag capped at `0.3`, `0.2` if the connecting edge has a relationship type (else 0), recency `max(0, 0.1 − 0.002×daysSinceModified)`, and `0.2 × cosineSimilarity` only when both leaves have embeddings (similarity clamped ≥0). `buildPromptContext` collects related leaves via BFS out to `depth` (default 2), then sorts them by relevance descending, then distance ascending. `pruneToTokenLimit` (maxTokens default 1000, estimate = `JSON.stringify(context).length/4`) does nothing if already under budget; otherwise, checking the estimate after each step and stopping early once under budget, it: 1) filters `related` to entries with relevance ≥ 0.5 (re-sorted by relevance desc first), 2) slices `related` to at most 3 entries, 3) deletes `core.tags`. If still over budget after step 3, the context is returned as-is regardless.

In scoreContextRelevance, relevance = 1/max(distance,1) [inverse graph distance] + min(sharedTagCount * 0.15, 0.3) [shared tags, capped] + (0.2 if the connecting edge has a relationship type, else 0) + max(0, 0.1 - ageDays*0.002) [recency, floored at 0] + max(0, cosineSimilarity)*0.2 [only when both leaves have embeddings], with the total capped at 1 and rounded to 3 decimals. buildPromptContext sorts related leaves by relevance desc (then distance asc) and passes the context to pruneToTokenLimit, which only touches anything if the JSON size already exceeds maxTokens, then applies steps in order, re-estimating tokens and returning as soon as it fits under maxTokens: (1) re-sort related by relevance desc and filter to keep only entries with relevance >= 0.5; (2) slice the remaining related array down to the top 3; (3) delete the `tags` field from the core leaf; it then returns the clone regardless of whether it is still over budget.

answer: Seven public methods change `leaves`, `tags`, or the `stem` connections in memory but contain no call to `saveData()` anywhere in their body, so autoSave never persists them: `addTags`, `renameTag`, and the import family `importData`, `importObject`, `importFromJSON`, `importFromCSV`, plus the `processCsvImport` helper the CSV import uses. `loadData()` is a related edge case: when the data file exists it only calls `importData` (no save), but when the file is missing it falls back to `initializeDefaultData()`, which does save. Every other mutating method (`addLeaf`, `removeLeaf`, `deleteLeaf`, `tagLeaf`, `connectLeaves`, `connectDirectedLeaves`, `updateLeaf`, `initializeDefaultData`, `clearAllData`) calls `saveData()` itself (directly or via `if (this.autoSave)`) and writes the file whenever `autoSave` is true. Note: the repo's knowledge-tree note for src/Rosemary.js and its cached "answers" entry are stale/outdated on this point — they list only addTags/importData/importObject/importFromJSON/importFromCSV and omit `renameTag`, which the current source shows also never saves; this was confirmed by reading the live source directly rather than the cache.

`Rosemary#connectLeaves` (src/Rosemary.js:258) is the shared core: it throws `Error('Leaf with id <id> not found')` when either id is not a key in the `leaves` Map — this also covers a missing/undefined id, since `Map.has(undefined)` is simply false and produces "Leaf with id undefined not found" — it only `console.warn`s and returns (no throw, no connection made) when `leafId1 === leafId2`, and treats `relationshipType` as optional, defaulting to `''` with no validation before storing it via `stem.addConnection`. The CLI's `connect <id1> <id2>` command (src/cli.js:92-104) declares both ids as required positional arguments in commander, so a truly omitted id is rejected by commander itself before the action runs; when both are present it calls `connectLeaves` in a try/catch, so an unknown id's error is caught and printed in red, while a duplicate-id pair doesn't throw, so the CLI still prints a "Connected leaf X and leaf Y" success message and calls `saveData()` even though nothing was connected; the type comes from `-r/--relationship`, defaulting to `''`. `POST /api/v1/connect` (src/api.js:89-97) destructures `id1, id2, type` from `req.body` and passes them straight through: a missing id is `undefined` and triggers the same "not found" error as an unknown id, both caught and returned as HTTP 400 `{error: message}`; a duplicate-id pair again doesn't throw inside `connectLeaves`, so the endpoint still responds 200 `{"message":"Leaves connected successfully"}` despite no connection being made; `type` is passed straight through as `relationshipType` with no server-side validation.

Only `Rosemary#connectLeaves` validates anything: it first compares the two ids and, if equal (a real duplicate or two ids that are both `undefined`), logs "Cannot connect a leaf to itself." and returns without connecting or throwing; otherwise it checks each id against `this.leaves` and throws `Leaf with id X not found` for any id not present, and it stores the relationship type exactly as given, defaulting to `''` when omitted/undefined (JS default parameters apply even when the caller passes `undefined` explicitly), with no format validation. The CLI's `connect <id1> <id2>` requires both ids as positional arguments, so commander itself rejects a missing id before `connectLeaves` runs; on a thrown "not found" error the CLI just does `console.error(chalk.red(...))` with no `process.exit`, so it still exits 0, while a same-id call or a real success both print a green "Connected leaf..." message, and `-r/--relationship` is passed through unchanged (empty-string default). `POST /api/v1/connect` destructures `id1, id2, type` from the JSON body with no presence checks and awaits `connectLeaves(id1, id2, type)`: two missing ids are both `undefined` so they compare equal and the route returns 200 "Leaves connected successfully" with nothing actually connected, exactly one missing id behaves like any unknown id and returns 400 with the "not found" message, a genuinely unknown id also returns 400, and any supplied/omitted `type` is forwarded untouched (defaulting to `''` in `connectLeaves` when absent).

All three layers call `Rosemary#connectLeaves(leafId1, leafId2, relationshipType='')`, which checks same-id first (leafId1===leafId2 → console.warn "Cannot connect a leaf to itself." and returns, no throw) then unknown-id (throws "Leaf with id X not found" if either leaf is missing from `this.leaves`), and never validates the relationship type—it's stored as given (default `''`) via `Stem#addConnection` with no check against the edges.js vocabulary. The CLI's `connect <id1> <id2>` is a commander required-argument command, so a missing id is rejected by commander before `connectLeaves` ever runs; for an unknown id or a thrown error, the CLI's try/catch just does `console.error(chalk.red(error.message))` and falls through to exit 0, while success (including the same-id no-op) prints "Connected..." and calls `brain.saveData()`. The REST route `POST /api/v1/connect` destructures `{id1, id2, type}` from the body with no validation, so a missing id becomes `undefined`: two missing ids make `undefined===undefined` true and hit the same-id branch (200 success, nothing connected), while one missing id fails the leaf lookup and returns 400 with the "not found" message; an unknown id also returns 400, and any given `type` (or `undefined`, defaulting to `''`) is passed through unchecked. This matches a stale standing note (`q:connect`, flagged stale because src/cli.js and src/Rosemary.js changed since it was written) that I verified against current source and found still accurate.

`npm run release -- patch` (npm script in package.json) runs scripts/release.js, which first refuses if `git status --porcelain` is dirty or the branch isn't `main` (via `git rev-parse --abbrev-ref HEAD`, overridable with `--force-branch`), then runs `npm test`, then runs `npm version patch` (bumps package.json's version and creates git tag `v<version>` in one commit, message `chore(release): %s`), then runs `git push --follow-tags`, then runs `npm publish`. `npm publish` triggers the `prepublishOnly` script in package.json (`npm test && node scripts/check-release.js`), which reruns Jest and then scripts/check-release.js, the final guard checking: working tree clean, HEAD matches tag `v<version>`, that tag is present on `origin` (`git ls-remote --tags origin`), the version isn't already on the npm registry (`npm view <name> versions --json`), and CHANGELOG.md mentions the new version. Only after check-release.js exits 0 does npm actually upload the package to the registry.

`npm run release -- patch` runs the "release" script in package.json, which is `scripts/release.js`; it first validates the bump argument, requires a clean tree (`git status --porcelain`) and branch `main` (`git rev-parse --abbrev-ref HEAD`, unless `--force-branch`). It then runs `npm test --silent` (the "test" script, Jest), runs `npm version patch -m "chore(release): %s"` to bump package.json and create the commit and tag `v<version>`, and runs `git push --follow-tags`. Finally release.js runs `npm publish`, which triggers the "prepublishOnly" script in package.json (`npm test && node scripts/check-release.js`). `scripts/check-release.js` re-checks name/version present, clean tree, that HEAD carries tag `v<version>`, that the tag is on origin, that the version isn't already on the npm registry (`npm view <name> versions --json`), and that `CHANGELOG.md` mentions the version, failing at the first mismatch. If check-release.js and the re-run tests pass, `npm publish` uploads the package to the npm registry, completing the release.

`npm run release -- patch` invokes scripts/release.js, which first validates the bump argument, requires a clean working tree (`git status --porcelain`), and requires the `main` branch unless `--force-branch` (`--dry-run` stops here). It then runs `npm test --silent`, then `npm version patch -m "chore(release): %s"` to bump package.json, commit, and tag `v<version>`, then `git push --follow-tags`, then `npm publish`. `npm publish` triggers the `prepublishOnly` script defined in package.json, which reruns `npm test` and then scripts/check-release.js. scripts/check-release.js checks that name/version are present, the tree is clean, the branch is only printed (not gated), the tag `v<version>` exists at HEAD and on origin, the version is not already on npm, and CHANGELOG.md mentions the new version — only after all of that does npm actually publish the package.

`scoreContextRelevance` (called per related leaf inside `buildPromptContext`) sums five weighted components, capped at 1 and rounded to 3 decimals: distanceScore = 1/max(distance,1) (inverse-distance, no fixed weight); tagScore = min(sharedTags * 0.15, 0.3) (0.15 per shared tag, capped at 0.3); relationshipScore = 0.2 if a relationship/edge type exists, else 0; recencyScore = max(0, 0.1 - ageDays*0.002) (starts at 0.1, decays 0.002/day, floors at 0); semanticScore = cosineSimilarity(centerEmbedding, relatedEmbedding) * 0.2, only if both leaves have embeddings (else 0). `pruneToTokenLimit` then prunes in order: (1) deep-clone the context and estimate tokens (chars/4 via `estimateTokens`); if within `maxTokens`, return immediately; (2) sort `related` by relevance descending, then filter out entries with relevance < 0.5, re-estimate and return if now within budget; (3) hard-cap `related` to the first 3 entries via `slice(0,3)`, re-estimate and return if within budget; (4) delete `core.tags` and return the result regardless of the final size.

scoreContextRelevance sums five weighted components and caps the total at 1: 1/distance (distance score), 0.15 per shared tag capped at 0.3 (tag score), 0.2 if the connecting edge has a relationship type (relationship score), a recency score of max(0, 0.1 − 0.002×ageDays) based on the related leaf's lastModified/createdAt, and cosineSimilarity×0.2 when both the center and related leaf have embeddings (else 0); the sum is rounded to 3 decimals and clamped with Math.min(1, ...). Related leaves come from a breadth-first walk to `depth` (default 2) and are sorted by relevance descending, then distance ascending, before pruneToTokenLimit(context, maxTokens) (maxTokens default 1000) runs. Pruning only proceeds if estimateTokens (JSON.stringify(context).length / 4) exceeds maxTokens, and then goes in order: (1) re-sort related by relevance descending, (2) filter out related leaves with relevance < 0.5, re-estimating after; (3) if still over budget, slice related down to the top 3, re-estimating again; (4) if still over budget, delete core.tags. The context (pruned or not) is returned at that point even if it is still over maxTokens.

`scoreContextRelevance` sums five components, then clamps to 1 and rounds to 3 decimals: distanceScore = 1/max(distance,1) (weight 1, no multiplier), tagScore = min(sharedTags*0.15, 0.3) (0.15 per shared tag, capped 0.3), relationshipScore = 0.2 if a relationship exists else 0, recencyScore = max(0, 0.1 − ageDays*0.002) (max 0.1, decaying 0.002/day), and semanticScore = cosineSimilarity(centerEmbedding, relatedEmbedding)*0.2 (weight 0.2, only if both embeddings exist, else 0). `pruneToTokenLimit` estimates tokens as JSON.stringify(context).length/4 and returns immediately if ≤ maxTokens; otherwise it sorts `related` by relevance descending and filters to keep only entries with relevance ≥ 0.5, then re-checks the budget; if still over, it slices `related` down to the top 3 remaining entries and re-checks; if still over, it deletes `core.tags` and returns the clone unconditionally (no further reduction even if still over maxTokens).
